title: Cranberry Sauce

drivers.name: Competitor store opening across the street
drivers.evidence: No prior data on similar events; new competitive threat. Price increase and no promotion suggest demand may be sensitive. Historical post-promo drops are not relevant. Effect size is uncertain, so shrink toward 1.0.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 9.1. No holiday or promotion is scheduled, but a competitor opens across the street, which may reduce demand. The price is up 2.1% (to $2.91), which historically has not driven lift. Past Halloween weeks show a noise-adjusted x1.0 effect, so no uplift. The past promotion aftereffects show a 32% drop in the following week (noise-adjusted x1.0), suggesting no lasting impact. The competitor entry is a new, untested event with no prior data, so its effect is uncertain. The baseline already reflects high noise (81%), so we shrink the effect toward 1.0. The median multiplier is adjusted slightly downward for the competitor, with wide spreads due to low confidence.

brief:
PRODUCT: Cranberry Sauce | category Grocery | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-25 (2 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 2.91 (+2.1% vs regular price 2.85)
  planner notes: A competitor opens a store across the street this week

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 9.1 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 19.9 | 10%-90%: 1.9 - 17.3

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-81% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
